$$\delta_k(x)=x^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_k-\tfrac12\mu_k^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_k+\log\pi_k$$

Linear discriminant analysis: from Bayes' theorem to Fisher's criterion

One model, reached down two roads. Start from a generative story — each class is a Gaussian, and all of them share a shape — and Bayes' rule hands you a hyperplane. Start instead from a geometric question — which direction separates these clouds best? — and the same hyperplane appears. This document walks both routes and shows where they meet.

Bayes' theorem & the generative shift The shared-covariance assumption Why the boundary is linear Between- and within-class scatter Fisher's criterion

Module 1
The probabilistic foundation
1

The baseline you already have

Logistic regression models the boundary and nothing else. Naming what it does — and does not — do is the cleanest way into LDA.

Logistic regression is discriminative. It writes down the log-odds directly and assumes they are linear in the features:

$$\log\frac{P(Y=1\mid x)}{P(Y=0\mid x)}=\beta_0+\beta^{\top}x\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad P(Y=1\mid x)=\sigma\!\left(\beta_0+\beta^{\top}x\right).$$

Why the two forms are equivalent

The step from "the log-odds are linear" to "the posterior is a sigmoid" is usually asserted.

Name the two posteriors, writing \(z=\beta_0+\beta^{\top}x\) for the linear score:

$$A=P(Y=1\mid x)=\sigma(z),\qquad B=P(Y=0\mid x)=1-\sigma(z),\qquad \sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}} .$$
STEP 1 · SIMPLIFY \(1-\sigma(z)\)

Put the \(1\) over the same denominator and the numerator collapses:

$$B=1-\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}=\frac{\left(1+e^{-z}\right)-1}{1+e^{-z}}=\frac{e^{-z}}{1+e^{-z}} .$$

So \(A\) and \(B\) are two fractions sharing the denominator \(1+e^{-z}\), with numerators \(1\) and \(e^{-z}\).

STEP 2 · FORM THE ODDS \(A/B\)

Dividing one by the other, the shared denominator cancels:

$$\frac{A}{B}=\frac{\sigma(z)}{1-\sigma(z)} =\frac{\dfrac{1}{1+e^{-z}}}{\dfrac{e^{-z}}{1+e^{-z}}} =\frac{1}{\cancel{1+e^{-z}}}\cdot\frac{\cancel{1+e^{-z}}}{e^{-z}} =\frac{1}{e^{-z}}=e^{z} .$$
STEP 3 · TAKE LOGARITHMS

\(\log\) and \(\exp\) are inverses, so the right-hand side collapses to \(z\):

$$\log\frac{A}{B}=\log e^{z}=z .$$
$$\log\frac{P(Y=1\mid x)}{P(Y=0\mid x)}=z=\beta_0+\beta^{\top}x .$$

Read in one direction, this says the sigmoid is exactly the function that turns a linear score into a probability whose log-odds are that score. Read in the other, it says that assuming linear log-odds forces the sigmoid — there was never a choice of squashing function to make.

Sub-topic — the logit, and what \(\beta_j\) means

The quantity \(\log\frac{p}{1-p}\) is called the logit of \(p\), and the derivation above shows it is the inverse of the sigmoid: \(\operatorname{logit}(\sigma(z))=z\). That is the origin of the name logistic regression, and it is why the model is described as a generalised linear model with a logit link.

It also fixes how to read a fitted coefficient. Since \(\log(A/B)\) is linear in \(x\), increasing \(x_j\) by one unit adds \(\beta_j\) to the log-odds, which multiplies the odds by \(e^{\beta_j}\). A coefficient of \(0.7\) means the odds roughly double; a coefficient of \(0\) means the feature leaves the odds untouched. Note this is a statement about odds, not about probability — the effect on \(P(Y=1\mid x)\) itself depends on where you start, which is why the sigmoid is steep in the middle and flat at the ends.

The coefficients are fitted by maximising the conditional likelihood \(\prod_i P(y_i\mid x_i)\). Nothing in that objective describes where the \(x\)'s came from. The model has no opinion about what a typical class-1 point looks like; it only knows which side of a hyperplane to put it on.

2

The generative shift

Model how each class produces its data, then invert with Bayes' theorem.

A name collision worth clearing up first

LDA here is linear discriminant analysis, a supervised classifier from 1936. It is unrelated to latent Dirichlet allocation, the unsupervised topic model students meet in NLP, which unfortunately shares the acronym.

Rather than modelling \(P(\text{class}\mid\text{data})\), we model how the data arises within each class and let Bayes' theorem do the inversion:

$$P(\text{Class}\mid\text{Data})=\frac{P(\text{Data}\mid\text{Class})\times P(\text{Class})}{P(\text{Data})}$$

In the notation used throughout the rest of this document, for classes \(k=1,\dots,K\):

$$P(Y=k\mid X=x)=\frac{f_k(x)\,\pi_k}{\displaystyle\sum_{\ell=1}^{K} f_\ell(x)\,\pi_\ell}$$
Why this is more than a change of notation

A generative model commits to a full description of the world, so it can do things a discriminative model cannot: sample new points, score how unusual an \(x\) is through \(P(x)\), marginalise over missing features, and make use of unlabelled data. The price is that it must get \(f_k(x)\) roughly right, and that is a much stronger commitment than getting a boundary right.

3

The three ingredients

Every term in Bayes' theorem has a name, a symbol, and a job.

TermSymbolWhat it isHow it is estimated
Prior\(\pi_k = P(Y=k)\) How common class \(k\) is before any feature is seen \(\hat\pi_k = n_k/n\), the proportion of training points in class \(k\)
Class-conditional density\(f_k(x) = P(X=x\mid Y=k)\) What class \(k\)'s points look like Depends entirely on the family chosen — block 4
Evidence / marginal\(P(x)=\sum_\ell f_\ell(x)\pi_\ell\) How likely \(x\) is under any class at all Not estimated separately — it falls out of the other two
The denominator is a normaliser, not an obstacle

\(P(x)\) is the same for every class, so it cannot change which class wins. Every comparison below therefore drops it, and \(P(Y=k\mid x)\propto f_k(x)\pi_k\) is all we ever need. It only has to be computed when you want a calibrated probability rather than a label, and even then it is just the sum of the numerators — the law of total probability, since the classes are exhaustive.

4

Choosing the class-conditional density

The behaviour of the classifier is decided almost entirely by the functional form picked for \(f_k(x)\). Bayes' theorem is the same in every case.

Choice of \(f_k(x)\)AssumptionResulting classifier
\(\prod_{j=1}^{p} f_{kj}(x_j)\) Features conditionally independent given the class Naive Bayes — cheap, \(O(p)\) parameters, ignores all correlation
\(\mathcal{N}(x;\mu_k,\Sigma)\), shared \(\Sigma\) One Gaussian per class, all sharing a shape LDA — linear boundary
\(\mathcal{N}(x;\mu_k,\Sigma_k)\) One Gaussian per class, shapes free QDA — quadratic boundary

Counting the parameters

The choice between these models is, at bottom, a parameter-counting argument. Taking a concrete case — \(p=50\) features, \(K=5\) classes:

Model Covariance Means Weights Total
Gaussian NB (per-class diagonal) 250250— 504
LDA 1,275250— 1,529
QDA 6,375250— 6,629

Every total also includes the \(K-1=4\) free class priors, which have no column of their own because they are the same in all four rows. The fifth prior is determined by the other four, since they must sum to one.

Where each number comes from

Gaussian naive Bayes — per-class diagonal
  • Covariance, 250. Conditional independence given the class forces every \(\Sigma_k\) to be diagonal, so only the \(p\) variances are estimated and all the off-diagonal correlations are set to zero. Each class gets its own set: \(K\times p=5\times 50=250\).
  • Means, 250. One centre per feature per class: \(K\times p=250\).
  • Total, 504. \(250+250+4\).
LDA — one shared full covariance
  • Covariance, 1,275. A single \(\Sigma\) shared by all classes, with the correlations kept. Symmetry means only the upper triangle is free: \(p(p+1)/2 = 50\times 51/2 = 1{,}275\).
  • Means, 250. Unchanged — sharing \(\Sigma\) does not mean sharing \(\mu_k\).
  • Total, 1,529. \(1{,}275+250+4\).
QDA — one full covariance per class
  • Covariance, 6,375. The shared-covariance assumption is dropped, so each class carries its own full matrix: \(K\times p(p+1)/2 = 5\times 1{,}275 = 6{,}375\).
  • Means, 250. Unchanged.
  • Total, 6,629. \(6{,}375+250+4\).
Reading the column that matters

The means column is nearly constant and the priors are negligible; almost the entire spread comes from the covariance column, which runs from 250 to 19,125. That is the whole LDA-versus-QDA trade-off in one number. Note also that each covariance parameter is estimated from a different amount of data: LDA's single \(\Sigma\) pools all \(n\) points, while each of QDA's five matrices sees only the \(n_k\) points of its own class.

Module 2
The Gaussian assumption and linear boundaries
5

The multivariate Gaussian

Two parameters per class: where the cloud sits, and what shape it has.

$$f_k(x)=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{p/2}\,|\Sigma_k|^{1/2}}\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12\,(x-\mu_k)^{\top}\Sigma_k^{-1}(x-\mu_k)\right),\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}^{p}.$$
$$\underbrace{(x-\mu_k)^{\top}\Sigma_k^{-1}(x-\mu_k)}_{\textstyle \text{squared Mahalanobis distance } D^2}$$
\(\mu_k\) — THE MEANA point in \(\mathbb{R}^p\). Moving it slides the whole cloud without changing its shape.
\(\Sigma_k\) — THE COVARIANCEA \(p\times p\) symmetric positive-definite matrix. Its eigenvectors give the axes of the elliptical contours and its eigenvalues give their squared lengths.

Everything that follows turns on one observation: the density depends on \(x\) only through that quadratic form. Contours of constant density are contours of constant Mahalanobis distance, which are ellipses centred at \(\mu_k\). And \(-\tfrac12 D^2\) is the only place \(x\) appears in \(\log f_k(x)\):

$$\log f_k(x) = -\tfrac{p}{2}\log(2\pi)-\tfrac12\log|\Sigma_k|-\tfrac12 (x-\mu_k)^{\top}\Sigma_k^{-1}(x-\mu_k).$$
Reading \(\Sigma\) off a picture

Diagonal \(\Sigma\) with equal entries → circular contours. Diagonal with unequal entries → ellipses aligned to the axes (this is the Gaussian naive Bayes case). Non-zero off-diagonal entries → tilted ellipses, and the tilt is exactly the correlation between features. A student who can look at a scatter plot and sketch \(\Sigma\) has understood the parameter.

6

The core LDA assumption

All classes share the same covariance matrix. You may move the ellipses; you may not reshape or rotate them.

$$\Sigma_k=\Sigma\quad\text{for every class }k.$$

Geometrically the assumption is easy to state and easy to check by eye. Every class gets its own centre \(\mu_k\), but all the ellipses are congruent: same size, same elongation, same orientation. Drop the assumption and each class picks its own shape.

Interactive · shared versus independent covariance

Both classes are fully adjustable. In LDA, \(\Sigma_2\) is locked to \(\Sigma_1\) — move Class 1’s covariance and both ellipses change together, which is the assumption made tangible. In QDA the lock is released and each class carries its own shape. The decision function underneath is recomputed from the sliders, not pre-baked.

μ₂ y1.1

7

Deriving the boundary

Set the log-odds between two classes to zero and watch the quadratic terms cancel.

The boundary between classes \(k\) and \(\ell\) is the set of points where the two posteriors are equal, that is where their ratio is \(1\) and its logarithm is \(0\). Since \(P(x)\) is shared it cancels immediately:

STEP 1 · WRITE THE LOG-ODDS

The evidence \(P(x)\) is common to both posteriors, so it cancels before we start:

$$\log\frac{P(Y=k\mid x)}{P(Y=\ell\mid x)} =\log\frac{f_k(x)\pi_k}{f_\ell(x)\pi_\ell} =\log\frac{f_k(x)}{f_\ell(x)}+\log\frac{\pi_k}{\pi_\ell}.$$
STEP 2 · SUBSTITUTE THE GAUSSIAN DENSITIES

Because \(\Sigma_k=\Sigma_\ell=\Sigma\), the normalising constants \((2\pi)^{-p/2}|\Sigma|^{-1/2}\) are identical in numerator and denominator and cancel in the ratio. Only the exponents survive:

$$\begin{aligned} =\ \log\frac{\pi_k}{\pi_\ell} &-\tfrac12(x-\mu_k)^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu_k)\\[2pt] &+\tfrac12(x-\mu_\ell)^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu_\ell). \end{aligned}$$
STEP 3 · EXPAND BOTH QUADRATIC FORMS

Using the symmetry of \(\Sigma^{-1}\), \((x-\mu)^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)=x^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}x-2x^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu+\mu^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu\):

$$\begin{aligned} =\ \log\frac{\pi_k}{\pi_\ell} &-\tfrac12\Big[\textcolor{#B23A6B}{x^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}x}-2x^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_k+\mu_k^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_k\Big]\\[2pt] &+\tfrac12\Big[\textcolor{#B23A6B}{x^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}x}-2x^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_\ell+\mu_\ell^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_\ell\Big]. \end{aligned}$$
STEP 4 · THE QUADRATIC TERMS CANCEL

The two terms in rose are identical, and they carry opposite signs. This is the whole trick, and it works only because the same \(\Sigma^{-1}\) sits in both. What remains is linear in \(x\):

$$\log\frac{P(Y=k\mid x)}{P(Y=\ell\mid x)} = x^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_k-\mu_\ell) -\tfrac12\left(\mu_k^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_k-\mu_\ell^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_\ell\right) +\log\frac{\pi_k}{\pi_\ell}.$$
STEP 5 · READ OFF THE HYPERPLANE

Setting the log-odds to zero gives \(w^{\top}x+b=0\), the equation of a hyperplane, with

$$w=\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_k-\mu_\ell),\qquad b=-\tfrac12(\mu_k+\mu_\ell)^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_k-\mu_\ell)+\log\frac{\pi_k}{\pi_\ell}.$$

From the log-odds to \(w\) and \(b\)

The derivation above ends with a linear function of \(x\). Turning that into the familiar \(w^{\top}x+b=0\) takes five short steps, and the last one pays off with a piece of geometry worth putting on the board.

STEP 1 · THE LOG-ODDS, IN THREE PIECES

Because LDA assumes every class shares the same \(\Sigma\), the quadratic terms \(x^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}x\) cancel and what is left is strictly linear in \(x\):

$$\log\frac{P(Y=k\mid x)}{P(Y=\ell\mid x)} = x^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_k-\mu_\ell) -\tfrac12\!\left(\mu_k^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_k-\mu_\ell^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_\ell\right) +\log\frac{\pi_k}{\pi_\ell}$$

Three distinct components, and it is worth naming them before going further:

  • a term that depends on the data point \(x\): \(\;x^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_k-\mu_\ell)\);
  • a constant built from the class means: \(\;-\tfrac12\!\left(\mu_k^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_k-\mu_\ell^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_\ell\right)\);
  • a constant built from the class priors: \(\;\log\dfrac{\pi_k}{\pi_\ell}\).
STEP 2 · DEFINE THE HYPERPLANE

The boundary is the set of points where the model is equally willing to predict class \(k\) or class \(\ell\) — that is, where the log-odds are zero. Setting the expression above to zero gives the standard equation of a hyperplane,

$$w^{\top}x+b=0,$$

so all that remains is bookkeeping: the \(x\)-dependent part becomes \(w\), and everything constant is bundled into \(b\).

STEP 3 · EXTRACT THE WEIGHT VECTOR

The part attached to \(x\) is \(x^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_k-\mu_\ell)\). Define

$$w=\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_k-\mu_\ell)$$

and that term is simply \(x^{\top}w\). Since \(x^{\top}w\) is a single number, it equals its own transpose, so \(x^{\top}w=w^{\top}x\) — which is exactly the form the hyperplane equation wants.

STEP 4 · FACTOR THE BIAS TERM

The leftover constants make up \(b\):

$$b=-\tfrac12\!\left(\mu_k^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_k-\mu_\ell^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_\ell\right)+\log\frac{\pi_k}{\pi_\ell}$$

That first bracket is a difference of two quadratic forms, and it factorises like a difference of squares. The claim to prove:

$$\mu_k^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_k-\mu_\ell^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_\ell =(\mu_k+\mu_\ell)^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_k-\mu_\ell)$$

Expand the right-hand side:

  1. Distribute the transpose. \((\mu_k+\mu_\ell)^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_k-\mu_\ell)=(\mu_k^{\top}+\mu_\ell^{\top})\,\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_k-\mu_\ell)\).
  2. Multiply out all four products. $$\mu_k^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_k \;\textcolor{#B23A6B}{-\;\mu_k^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_\ell} \;\textcolor{#B23A6B}{+\;\mu_\ell^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_k} \;-\;\mu_\ell^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_\ell$$
  3. Apply symmetry to the cross-terms. Each of \(\mu_k^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_\ell\) and \(\mu_\ell^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_k\) is a scalar, so each equals its own transpose; and transposing one gives the other precisely because \(\Sigma^{-1}\) is symmetric. The two are therefore the same number.
  4. They cancel. One enters with a minus sign and the other with a plus, so the two terms in rose sum to zero.
  5. What remains is \(\mu_k^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_k-\mu_\ell^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_\ell\), which is what we set out to match.

Substituting the compact form back:

$$b=-\tfrac12(\mu_k+\mu_\ell)^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_k-\mu_\ell)+\log\frac{\pi_k}{\pi_\ell}$$
STEP 5 · THE GEOMETRIC PAYOFF

Notice that \(\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_k-\mu_\ell)\) appearing inside \(b\) is exactly \(w\). Rewriting the boundary equation with that substitution:

$$w^{\top}x-\tfrac12(\mu_k+\mu_\ell)^{\top}w+\log\frac{\pi_k}{\pi_\ell}=0$$

and since \((\mu_k+\mu_\ell)^{\top}w=w^{\top}(\mu_k+\mu_\ell)\), both terms carry a \(w^{\top}\) and it factors out:

$$w^{\top}\!\left(x-\tfrac12(\mu_k+\mu_\ell)\right)+\log\frac{\pi_k}{\pi_\ell}=0$$

If the two priors are equal the ratio is \(1\), its logarithm is \(0\), and the equation collapses to

$$w^{\top}\!\left(x-\tfrac12(\mu_k+\mu_\ell)\right)=0 .$$

\(\tfrac12(\mu_k+\mu_\ell)\) is the midpoint between the two class means. Substituting \(x=\) midpoint gives \(w^{\top}\mathbf{0}=0\), which holds. So with equal priors, the boundary always passes exactly through the midpoint of the two means.

What this does and does not pin down

The factored form separates the two things a hyperplane needs. \(w\) fixes its orientation; the point it passes through fixes its position. Equal priors put that point at the midpoint. Unequal priors add \(\log(\pi_k/\pi_\ell)\), which slides the plane along \(w\) without rotating it — towards the rarer class, enlarging the common one's region.

What the midpoint result does not say is that the boundary is perpendicular to the segment joining the means. It passes through that segment's midpoint, but its normal is \(\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_k-\mu_\ell)\), not \(\mu_k-\mu_\ell\). The two coincide only when \(\Sigma\) is a multiple of the identity. Passing through the midpoint and being perpendicular to the segment are independent claims, and LDA guarantees only the first.

The perpendicular-bisector misconception

The misconception

Draw a line from the centre of Class 1 to the centre of Class 2. The intuition says the decision boundary cuts that line exactly in half, at a strict \(90^\circ\) angle — a perpendicular bisector. It feels obviously right: each point on such a line is equidistant from both means, so surely the classifier is undecided there.

Half of that is true. The boundary does pass through the midpoint when the priors are equal. The perpendicularity is what fails.

The mathematical reality

The orientation of the boundary is set by its normal vector, and block 7 derived what that is:

$$w=\textcolor{#1F8A85}{\Sigma^{-1}}\big(\mu_k-\mu_\ell\big) \qquad\text{not}\qquad w=\big(\mu_k-\mu_\ell\big)$$
THE FACTOR THAT IS FORGOTTENThe misconception silently drops \(\Sigma^{-1}\) and takes the raw difference of the means as the normal. Everything below is a consequence of putting it back.

What \(\Sigma^{-1}\) does to the direction

THE RARE CASE — \(\Sigma=\sigma^2 I\)
  • The clusters are perfectly spherical: equal variance in every direction, zero correlation between features.
  • \(\Sigma^{-1}=\sigma^{-2}I\) is a scalar multiple of the identity, and multiplying a vector by a scalar cannot change its direction.
  • So \(w\propto\mu_k-\mu_\ell\), and the boundary genuinely is the perpendicular bisector. The intuition is correct — here, and only here.
THE GENERAL CASE — ANY OTHER \(\Sigma\)
  • Real features are correlated, or measured on different scales, or both. The clusters are elliptical, not spherical.
  • \(\Sigma^{-1}\) is then a genuine linear map with unequal eigenvalues, and it rotates the vector it acts on.
  • So \(w\) points somewhere other than \(\mu_k-\mu_\ell\), and the boundary is tilted away from the perpendicular bisector.
Why the tilt is the right thing to do

The rotation is not a defect to be corrected — it is the classifier doing its job. A perpendicular bisector treats every direction in feature space as equally informative. LDA knows better: it has estimated \(\Sigma\), so it knows which directions the data varies a lot in and which it barely varies in at all. Movement along a high-variance direction is weak evidence; movement along a low-variance direction is strong evidence. \(\Sigma^{-1}\) is precisely the operator that discounts the former and amplifies the latter, and the resulting tilt is the boundary accounting for the shape of the data rather than blindly walling off the space between two centres.

Equivalently: LDA is nearest-mean classification under the Mahalanobis metric, not the Euclidean one. The perpendicular bisector is the right answer to the Euclidean question, which is simply not the question being asked.

8

The discriminant function

With \(K\) classes, pairwise comparisons are clumsy. One score per class is cleaner and gives the method its name.

Anything that appears identically in every class's log-posterior can be dropped, because it cannot change the argmax. Starting from \(\log\big(f_k(x)\pi_k\big)\) and discarding \(-\tfrac{p}{2}\log 2\pi\), \(-\tfrac12\log|\Sigma|\) and \(-\tfrac12 x^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}x\) — all class-independent under the shared-\(\Sigma\) assumption — leaves the linear discriminant function:

$$\delta_k(x)=x^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_k-\tfrac12\,\mu_k^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_k+\log\pi_k, \qquad \hat y(x)=\arg\max_{k}\ \delta_k(x).$$

Each \(\delta_k\) is an affine function of \(x\), which is where "linear discriminant analysis" comes from. The decision regions are intersections of half-spaces, so every region is a convex polyhedron and every pairwise boundary is a piece of a hyperplane.

Deriving \(\delta_k(x)\) by discarding what cannot decide anything

The discriminant function is not a new object — it is \(\log\!\big(f_k(x)\,\pi_k\big)\) with every term that is the same for all classes thrown away. Four steps, and the only tool is the observation that adding a constant to every score leaves the winner unchanged.

The licence for every deletion below

We are going to choose \(\hat y=\arg\max_k\ \text{score}_k(x)\). If \(C(x)\) does not depend on \(k\), then

$$\arg\max_k\ \big[\text{score}_k(x)+C(x)\big]=\arg\max_k\ \text{score}_k(x),$$

because \(C(x)\) shifts all \(K\) scores by the same amount and so cannot reorder them. Every term struck out below is of exactly this kind. Note the scores themselves change — only their ranking is preserved, which is all a classifier needs.

STEP 1 · TAKE THE LOG OF THE GAUSSIAN DENSITY

Logs turn the product-and-exponential into a sum, and the exponent drops down intact:

$$\log f_k(x)= \underbrace{-\tfrac{p}{2}\log(2\pi)}_{\textcolor{#B23A6B}{\text{no }k}} \;\underbrace{-\tfrac12\log|\Sigma|}_{\textcolor{#B23A6B}{\text{no }k}} \;-\tfrac12(x-\mu_k)^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu_k)$$

The first term involves only the dimension \(p\). The second involves only \(\Sigma\) — and under the LDA assumption there is just one \(\Sigma\), shared by every class, so it carries no \(k\) either. Both are class-independent and both go.

This is the first place the shared-covariance assumption earns its keep. In QDA each class has its own \(\Sigma_k\), the term becomes \(-\tfrac12\log|\Sigma_k|\), and it must be kept.

STEP 2 · EXPAND THE QUADRATIC FORM

What survives is \(-\tfrac12(x-\mu_k)^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu_k)\). Multiplying out, and using the symmetry of \(\Sigma^{-1}\) to combine the two identical cross-terms into one:

$$=-\tfrac12\Big[\, \underbrace{x^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}x}_{\textcolor{#B23A6B}{\text{no }k}} \;-\;2\,x^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_k \;+\;\mu_k^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_k \,\Big]$$

Three terms, and only the last two mention \(\mu_k\). The first depends on the test point and on \(\Sigma\), but not on which class we are scoring — so it goes too.

STEP 3 · WHAT IS LEFT $$=-\tfrac12\Big[-2\,x^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_k+\mu_k^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_k\Big]$$

Distributing the \(-\tfrac12\) across the bracket flips both signs and halves the second term:

$$=x^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_k-\tfrac12\,\mu_k^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_k$$
STEP 4 · PUT THE PRIOR BACK

We wanted \(\log\!\big(f_k(x)\pi_k\big)=\log f_k(x)+\log\pi_k\), and \(\log\pi_k\) very much depends on \(k\), so it stays. Adding it to what survived gives the discriminant:

$$\delta_k(x)=x^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_k-\tfrac12\,\mu_k^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_k+\log\pi_k$$
$$\hat y(x)=\arg\max_{k}\ \log\!\big(f_k(x)\,\pi_k\big)=\arg\max_{k}\ \delta_k(x)$$
Two things to write carefully

The final argmax takes \(\delta_k\), not \(\log\delta_k\). It is tempting to carry the logarithm through to the end, but \(\delta_k(x)\) is already a log — it is what \(\log(f_k(x)\pi_k)\) reduced to. Writing \(\arg\max_k\log\delta_k(x)\) would take a second logarithm, and since \(\delta_k\) is freely negative that expression is often undefined.

The chain of equalities is really a proportionality. Strictly, \(\delta_k(x)=\log\!\big(f_k(x)\pi_k\big)+C(x)\) for the class-independent constant \(C(x)=\tfrac{p}{2}\log 2\pi+\tfrac12\log|\Sigma|+\tfrac12x^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}x\) that we discarded. The two are not equal — they differ by \(C(x)\) at every point — but they have the same argmax, which is the only property being used. If you need an actual probability rather than a label, you cannot use \(\delta_k\); go back to \(f_k(x)\pi_k\) and normalise.

Why the result is worth the effort

Look at what the three surviving terms are made of. \(x\) appears exactly once, linearly, in \(x^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_k\). The other two terms are constants computed once at training time. So each \(\delta_k\) is an affine function of \(x\) — which is where the word linear in linear discriminant analysis comes from, and why classifying a point costs one dot product per class rather than an exponential.

Reading the terms individually:

  • \(x^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_k\) rewards points lying in the direction of \(\mu_k\), measured in the whitened geometry \(\Sigma^{-1}\) defines rather than the raw Euclidean one.
  • \(-\tfrac12\mu_k^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}\mu_k\) penalises classes whose mean is far from the origin, correcting the bias the first term would otherwise have towards distant means.
  • \(\log\pi_k\) tilts everything towards the common classes, by the same amount everywhere. Doubling a prior adds \(\log 2\approx0.69\) to that class's score regardless of \(x\).
Sub-topic — the same formula read as a distance

Undo step 2 rather than step 3 and you get an equivalent form that is sometimes more revealing:

$$\delta_k(x)=-\tfrac12(x-\mu_k)^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu_k)+\log\pi_k+\text{const}.$$

With equal priors, maximising this is minimising \((x-\mu_k)^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu_k)\) — the squared Mahalanobis distance to the class mean. So LDA with equal priors is exactly nearest class mean, provided distance is measured in the metric the data's own covariance defines. Unequal priors add a per-class bonus of \(\log\pi_k\) on top.

9

Contrast with QDA

Drop the shared-covariance assumption and step 4 of the derivation stops working.

If each class keeps its own \(\Sigma_k\), two things change in the derivation. The normalisers \(|\Sigma_k|^{-1/2}\) no longer cancel, and — decisively — the quadratic terms \(x^{\top}\Sigma_k^{-1}x\) differ between classes, so they survive:

$$\delta_k(x)=-\tfrac12\log|\Sigma_k|-\tfrac12(x-\mu_k)^{\top}\Sigma_k^{-1}(x-\mu_k)+\log\pi_k.$$

The pairwise boundary now contains a genuine quadratic form:

$$x^{\top}\underbrace{\tfrac12\left(\Sigma_\ell^{-1}-\Sigma_k^{-1}\right)}_{\textstyle A}x + w^{\top}x + b = 0,$$

and the solution set of such an equation is a conic: an ellipse, a parabola, a hyperbola, or in degenerate cases a line or a pair of lines. The moment \(A=0\) — that is, \(\Sigma_k=\Sigma_\ell\) — we are back to LDA.

LDAQDA
Covarianceone shared \(\Sigma\)one \(\Sigma_k\) per class
Covariance parameters\(p(p+1)/2\)\(K\,p(p+1)/2\)
Boundaryhyperplanequadric surface
Biashigherlower
Variancelowerhigher
Needs \(n_k > p\) per classno — pools everythingyes, or \(\hat\Sigma_k\) is singular

Why the QDA boundary is quadratic

The pairwise boundary between classes \(k\) and \(\ell\) is the set of points where the two discriminants agree — where \(\delta_k(x)=\delta_\ell(x)\), or equivalently \(\delta_k(x)-\delta_\ell(x)=0\). Under LDA that difference came out linear because two things cancelled. Drop the shared covariance and neither cancellation survives: the normalisers \(|\Sigma_k|^{-1/2}\) differ between classes, and so do the quadratic terms \(x^{\top}\Sigma_k^{-1}x\). Here is what is left.

STEP 1 · EXPAND THE DISCRIMINANT

Starting from

$$\delta_k(x)=-\tfrac12\log|\Sigma_k|-\tfrac12(x-\mu_k)^{\top}\Sigma_k^{-1}(x-\mu_k)+\log\pi_k,$$

expand the Mahalanobis term, using the symmetry of \(\Sigma_k^{-1}\) to merge the two cross-terms (\(x^{\top}\Sigma_k^{-1}\mu_k=\mu_k^{\top}\Sigma_k^{-1}x\)):

$$(x-\mu_k)^{\top}\Sigma_k^{-1}(x-\mu_k)=x^{\top}\Sigma_k^{-1}x-2x^{\top}\Sigma_k^{-1}\mu_k+\mu_k^{\top}\Sigma_k^{-1}\mu_k .$$

Substituting back and distributing the \(-\tfrac12\):

$$\delta_k(x)=-\tfrac12 x^{\top}\Sigma_k^{-1}x +x^{\top}\Sigma_k^{-1}\mu_k -\tfrac12\mu_k^{\top}\Sigma_k^{-1}\mu_k -\tfrac12\log|\Sigma_k|+\log\pi_k .$$
STEP 2 · SUBTRACT

Write the boundary condition out in full, one bracket per class:

$$\begin{aligned} &\left(-\tfrac12 x^{\top}\Sigma_k^{-1}x+x^{\top}\Sigma_k^{-1}\mu_k -\tfrac12\mu_k^{\top}\Sigma_k^{-1}\mu_k-\tfrac12\log|\Sigma_k|+\log\pi_k\right)\\[3pt] -\;&\left(-\tfrac12 x^{\top}\Sigma_\ell^{-1}x+x^{\top}\Sigma_\ell^{-1}\mu_\ell -\tfrac12\mu_\ell^{\top}\Sigma_\ell^{-1}\mu_\ell-\tfrac12\log|\Sigma_\ell|+\log\pi_\ell\right)=0 \end{aligned}$$

Nothing has cancelled. Under LDA the first terms of each bracket were identical and vanished here; with \(\Sigma_k\neq\Sigma_\ell\) they do not.

STEP 3 · GROUP BY POWERS OF \(x\)

Terms with \(x\) twice.

$$-\tfrac12 x^{\top}\Sigma_k^{-1}x-\left(-\tfrac12 x^{\top}\Sigma_\ell^{-1}x\right) =\tfrac12 x^{\top}\Sigma_\ell^{-1}x-\tfrac12 x^{\top}\Sigma_k^{-1}x =x^{\top}\underbrace{\left[\tfrac12\left(\Sigma_\ell^{-1}-\Sigma_k^{-1}\right)\right]}_{\textstyle A}x$$

Terms with \(x\) once.

$$x^{\top}\Sigma_k^{-1}\mu_k-x^{\top}\Sigma_\ell^{-1}\mu_\ell =x^{\top}\underbrace{\left(\Sigma_k^{-1}\mu_k-\Sigma_\ell^{-1}\mu_\ell\right)}_{\textstyle w} =w^{\top}x,$$

the last step because \(x^{\top}w\) is a scalar and so equals its own transpose.

Everything else.

$$b=-\tfrac12\mu_k^{\top}\Sigma_k^{-1}\mu_k+\tfrac12\mu_\ell^{\top}\Sigma_\ell^{-1}\mu_\ell -\tfrac12\log|\Sigma_k|+\tfrac12\log|\Sigma_\ell|+\log\frac{\pi_k}{\pi_\ell}$$
$$x^{\top}\underbrace{\tfrac12\left(\Sigma_\ell^{-1}-\Sigma_k^{-1}\right)}_{A}x+w^{\top}x+b=0$$
Where LDA sits inside this

Set \(\Sigma_k=\Sigma_\ell=\Sigma\). Then \(A=\tfrac12(\Sigma^{-1}-\Sigma^{-1})=0\), the quadratic form disappears, and what remains is \(w^{\top}x+b=0\) — a hyperplane. The log-determinant terms in \(b\) also cancel, since \(\log|\Sigma_k|=\log|\Sigma_\ell|\), which is why LDA's intercept has no such term. LDA is not a different model; it is QDA restricted to the slice of parameter space where \(A\) happens to vanish.

Reading \(w\) and \(b\) carefully

Both differ from their LDA counterparts in a way worth naming, because the symbols look the same:

  • In LDA, \(w=\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_k-\mu_\ell)\) — one inverse applied to the difference of the means. In QDA, \(w=\Sigma_k^{-1}\mu_k-\Sigma_\ell^{-1}\mu_\ell\) — each mean whitened by its own covariance, and only then subtracted. These coincide only when \(\Sigma_k=\Sigma_\ell\).
  • QDA's \(b\) carries \(-\tfrac12\log|\Sigma_k|+\tfrac12\log|\Sigma_\ell|\), a term with no LDA analogue. It is a volume penalty: a class with a large \(|\Sigma_k|\) spreads its probability mass thinly over a bigger region, so every individual point is less likely to have come from it, and the term docks its score accordingly.
10

Estimating the parameters

Three quantities, all from training data, all by maximum likelihood. One of them has a trap in it.

$$\hat\pi_k=\frac{n_k}{n},\qquad \hat\mu_k=\frac{1}{n_k}\sum_{i:\,y_i=k}x_i,\qquad \hat\Sigma=\frac{1}{n-K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\ \sum_{i:\,y_i=k}\left(x_i-\hat\mu_k\right)\left(x_i-\hat\mu_k\right)^{\top}.$$

The first two are unsurprising: class proportions and class means. The third is the pooled covariance, and it is where the mistakes happen.

The trap — subtract the class mean, never the global mean

Each point's deviation must be measured from its own class mean \(\hat\mu_k\), and only then are the contributions from all classes added together. Using the global mean \(\bar x\) instead folds the separation between the classes into what is supposed to measure spread within them, inflating \(\hat\Sigma\) and flattening the boundary towards the perpendicular bisector.

Formally: the total scatter decomposes as \(S_T = S_W + S_B\). Using the global mean computes \(S_T\) when you wanted \(S_W\); the error is exactly the between-class term of block 13.

Why the denominator is \(N-K\)

An estimator is unbiased when its expected value lands exactly on the quantity it is estimating: \(\mathbb{E}\!\left[\hat\sigma^2\right]=\sigma^2\), with no systematic tendency to run high or low. The claim is that \(N-K\) is the only denominator that achieves this, and it can be proved outright by computing \(\mathbb{E}[SS_W]\).

Setup and notation
  • \(N\) observations split across \(K\) classes, with \(n_k\) in class \(k\), so \(\sum_{k=1}^{K} n_k = N\).
  • \(X_{ik}\) is observation \(i\) of class \(k\); \(\mu_k\) is the class's true, unknown mean; \(\bar X_k\) is the sample mean we actually compute.
  • All classes share the same true variance \(\sigma^2\) — the LDA assumption.

The within-class sum of squares measures every point against its own sample mean:

$$SS_W=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i=1}^{n_k}\left(X_{ik}-\bar X_k\right)^2 .$$
STEP 1 · THE SAMPLE MEAN IS TOO FLATTERING

The trouble is that \(\mu_k\) is unknown, so we substitute \(\bar X_k\) — and a sample always clusters more tightly around its own mean than around the true one. To see how much, add and subtract \(\mu_k\):

$$\left(X_{ik}-\bar X_k\right)=\left(X_{ik}-\mu_k\right)-\left(\bar X_k-\mu_k\right).$$

Square it, as \((a-b)^2=a^2-2ab+b^2\), and sum over the \(n_k\) points of the class:

$$\sum_{i=1}^{n_k}\left(X_{ik}-\bar X_k\right)^2 =\sum_{i=1}^{n_k}\left(X_{ik}-\mu_k\right)^2 -2\left(\bar X_k-\mu_k\right)\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^{n_k}\left(X_{ik}-\mu_k\right)}_{\textstyle =\,n_k(\bar X_k-\mu_k)} +n_k\left(\bar X_k-\mu_k\right)^2 .$$

The braced sum is \(n_k(\bar X_k-\mu_k)\) by the definition of \(\bar X_k\), so the middle term is \(-2n_k(\bar X_k-\mu_k)^2\). Adding the last term leaves \(-n_k(\bar X_k-\mu_k)^2\):

$$\sum_{i=1}^{n_k}\left(X_{ik}-\bar X_k\right)^2 =\sum_{i=1}^{n_k}\left(X_{ik}-\mu_k\right)^2-n_k\left(\bar X_k-\mu_k\right)^2 .$$

Read it as an accounting identity: scatter about the sample mean equals scatter about the true mean, minus a strictly non-negative amount. The shortfall is the bias, and it is already visible before any expectation is taken.

STEP 2 · TAKE EXPECTATIONS, ONE CLASS AT A TIME

The honest part. \(\mathbb{E}\!\left[(X_{ik}-\mu_k)^2\right]\) is the definition of \(\sigma^2\), and there are \(n_k\) such terms:

$$\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{n_k}\left(X_{ik}-\mu_k\right)^2\right]=n_k\sigma^2 .$$

The penalty. \(\mathbb{E}\!\left[(\bar X_k-\mu_k)^2\right]\) is the variance of a sample mean, which is \(\sigma^2/n_k\). Multiplying by the \(n_k\) outside:

$$\mathbb{E}\!\left[n_k\left(\bar X_k-\mu_k\right)^2\right]=n_k\cdot\frac{\sigma^2}{n_k}=\sigma^2 .$$

Subtracting one from the other:

$$\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{n_k}\left(X_{ik}-\bar X_k\right)^2\right] =n_k\sigma^2-\sigma^2=(n_k-1)\,\sigma^2 .$$

There is the bias, exactly quantified. The scatter falls short of \(n_k\sigma^2\) by precisely one \(\sigma^2\), no matter how large the class — that is the degree of freedom spent on estimating \(\bar X_k\).

STEP 3 · SUM OVER THE CLASSES $$\mathbb{E}[SS_W]=\sum_{k=1}^{K}(n_k-1)\sigma^2 =\sigma^2\sum_{k=1}^{K}(n_k-1) =\sigma^2\left(\sum_{k=1}^{K}n_k-\sum_{k=1}^{K}1\right)$$

The first sum is \(N\); the second adds \(1\) exactly \(K\) times, giving \(K\). Hence

$$\mathbb{E}[SS_W]=(N-K)\,\sigma^2 .$$

One \(\sigma^2\) is lost per class, and there are \(K\) classes.

$$\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{SS_W}{N-K}\right]=\frac{(N-K)\sigma^2}{N-K}=\sigma^2$$

So \(N-K\) is not a convention or a safety margin — it is forced. Dividing by \(N\) instead would make the estimate systematically too small, understating the true spread of every class.

Checked by simulation

With \(K=4\) classes of sizes \(6,9,5,7\) (so \(N=27\)) drawn from a normal with \(\sigma^2=2.75\), averaged over 400,000 replications:

divide \(SS_W\) byexpected valueverdict
\(N=27\)2.342underestimates by 15%
\(N-1=26\)2.432still biased low
\(N-K=23\)2.749unbiased

Simulated \(\mathbb{E}[SS_W]=63.23\) against the predicted \((N-K)\sigma^2=63.25\).

The matrix version, which is what LDA actually uses

The argument above is written for a scalar variance, but nothing in it depends on that. Replace squares with outer products and the same cancellation runs through unchanged:

$$\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i:\,y_i=k}\left(x_i-\hat\mu_k\right)\left(x_i-\hat\mu_k\right)^{\top}\right]=(N-K)\,\Sigma,$$

so \(\hat\Sigma=SS_W/(N-K)\) is unbiased entry by entry, for the variances on the diagonal and the covariances off it alike. I confirmed this by simulation in \(\mathbb{R}^3\): the largest discrepancy between \(\mathbb{E}[SS_W]/(N-K)\) and the true \(\Sigma\) over all nine entries was \(0.014\).

Module 3
Fisher's linear discriminant — the projection view
11

Supervised dimensionality reduction

The same classifier, re-derived without a single probability. Fisher asks a geometric question instead.

Forget Gaussians for a moment. Suppose you must collapse \(p\)-dimensional data onto a single number and then separate the classes using only that number. Which direction should you project along?

This is a dimensionality-reduction question, similar to PCA. The two methods look superficially similar — both find a direction, both project onto it — and are completely different in what they optimise.

PCA — UNSUPERVISED
  • Maximises \(w^{\top}S_T\,w\), the total variance of the projected data.
  • Never looks at the labels. It would return the same direction if you shuffled every \(y_i\).
  • Answer: the top eigenvector of the total covariance.
  • Good for compression and denoising.
LDA / FISHER — SUPERVISED
  • Maximises separation between class means relative to the spread within classes.
  • Uses the labels at every step.
  • Answer: the top eigenvector of \(S_W^{-1}S_B\).
  • Good for classification and for plotting classes apart.
When PCA and LDA do agree

If the within-class scatter is isotropic — \(S_W\propto I\) — then the only structure left in the total scatter is the between-class separation, and the leading principal component lines up with \(\mu_1-\mu_2\). This is why PCA-before-classification often works adequately in practice, and also why it fails exactly when the features are correlated, which is most of the time.

12

Step 1 — define the projection

A direction \(w\) turns every \(p\)-dimensional point into one number.

$$y = w^{\top}x,\qquad w\in\mathbb{R}^{p}.$$

Under this map, the class means and covariances project too, and both projections are one line of algebra:

$$\tilde\mu_k = w^{\top}\mu_k,\qquad \widetilde{\operatorname{Var}}_k = w^{\top}\Sigma_k\,w .$$

What the projection actually does

The goal of this step is to take multi-dimensional points and flatten them onto a single number line, so that separating the classes becomes a one-dimensional problem. Three quantities come along for the ride.

$$y=w^{\top}x$$
\(w\) — THE DIRECTION OF THE LINENot a point and not a boundary: \(w\) names the direction of a new number line laid across the feature space.
\(y\) — WHERE \(x\) LANDS ON ITThe dot product drops the \(p\)-dimensional point straight down onto that line and reports the single number it hits.

Because the map is linear, the two things we care about — where each class sits, and how far it spreads — transform in one line each:

In \(p\) dimensionsProjected onto \(w\)What it means
class mean \(\mu_k\) \(\tilde\mu_k=w^{\top}\mu_k\) where that class's centre lands on the number line
covariance \(\Sigma_k\) \(\widetilde{\operatorname{Var}}_k=w^{\top}\Sigma_k\,w\) how wide the flattened cloud is once squashed onto the line
Why the spread formula has \(w\) on both sides

The mean is a point, so projecting it takes one dot product. Variance is a squared quantity, so it picks up the direction twice — once on each side of \(\Sigma_k\). That is the whole content of \(\operatorname{Var}(w^{\top}X)=w^{\top}\Sigma_k w\), and it is also why the next paragraph's scaling behaves the way it does.

Why \(w\) does not need a fixed length

Replace \(w\) by \(cw\) for any \(c\neq0\) — think of it as relabelling the ruler with finer or coarser tick marks. Everything on the line stretches together:

  • each projected mean \(\tilde\mu_k\) scales by \(c\), so the gap between the class centres scales by \(c\);
  • the projected variance carries \(w\) twice, so it scales by \(c^2\) — meaning the standard deviation also scales by \(c\).

The separation grows, which sounds like an improvement, but the spread grows by exactly the same factor and cancels the benefit precisely. Separation relative to spread never changes. Only the direction \(w\) points in carries any information; its length carries none.

The same numbers, on the document's own configuration
\(c\)gap \(\tilde\mu_1-\tilde\mu_2\) \(\widetilde{\operatorname{Var}}\) gap ÷ s.d.\(J(w)\)
0.51.2940.1073.95047.8030
12.5880.4293.95047.8030
25.1761.7173.95047.8030
512.94110.7313.95047.8030
2051.765171.7013.95047.8030

A fortyfold stretch of \(w\) multiplies the gap by 40 and the variance by 1,600 — and leaves the ratio, and therefore \(J\), identical to four decimal places.

There are two ways to deal with this indeterminacy:

OPTION 1 — PIN THE LENGTH
  • Impose \(\|w\|=1\), or the algebraically tidier \(w^{\top}S_W w=1\).
  • Turns the problem into a constrained optimisation, solved with a Lagrange multiplier.
  • Perfectly valid, and how the problem is often posed in textbooks.
OPTION 2 — BUILD A RATIO
  • Put the separation on top and the spread underneath.
  • Any factor \(c\) appears as \(c^2\) in both and cancels on its own.
  • No constraint needed at all — and this is the route Fisher's criterion takes.
What scale-invariance costs you later

Because \(J\) cannot see the length of \(w\), its solution is a direction and nothing more. It says which way to look, but not where along that line to place the cut between classes. That threshold has to come from somewhere else — from the Gaussian model with its priors, as in Module 2, or empirically from the projected training values. It is the one thing Fisher's criterion structurally cannot supply.

13

Step 2 — between-class scatter

Push the projected class means as far apart as possible.

For two classes, the natural thing to maximise is the squared gap between the projected means. Written out and then re-folded into a matrix:

STEP 1 · THE PROJECTED GAP, SQUARED $$\left(w^{\top}\mu_1-w^{\top}\mu_2\right)^2=\left(w^{\top}(\mu_1-\mu_2)\right)^2 .$$
STEP 2 · FOLD IT INTO A MATRIX

A scalar equals its own transpose, so \(\big(w^{\top}v\big)^2=\big(w^{\top}v\big)\big(v^{\top}w\big)\). Taking \(v=\mu_1-\mu_2\) and associating differently:

$$=w^{\top}\underbrace{(\mu_1-\mu_2)(\mu_1-\mu_2)^{\top}}_{\textstyle S_B}\,w = w^{\top}S_B\,w .$$
$$S_B=(\mu_1-\mu_2)(\mu_1-\mu_2)^{\top}\qquad\text{(between-class scatter matrix)}$$

From two classes to \(K\): building the bridge

The \(K\)-class formula for \(S_B\) introduces two things that appear from nowhere if it is stated straight after the two-class case: a global mean \(\bar x\), and class weights \(N_k\). Both are inevitable once you see that pushing two means apart and pushing both means away from their shared centre are the same operation. That is the bridge.

PHASE 1 · THE ANCHOR — TWO CLASSES

The instinct is to maximise the squared gap between the projected means, we derived earlier:

$$\left(w^{\top}\mu_1-w^{\top}\mu_2\right)^2 =w^{\top}\underbrace{(\mu_1-\mu_2)(\mu_1-\mu_2)^{\top}}_{\textstyle S_B}\,w .$$

Concrete, and entirely about the difference of the two means. No global centre anywhere in sight.

PHASE 2 · THE BRIDGE — SHIFT THE REFERENCE POINT

Now measure both means from the centre of the data instead of from each other. Take the balanced case first, \(N_1=N_2=N/2\), so the global mean is the midpoint:

$$\bar x=\frac{\mu_1+\mu_2}{2},\qquad \mu_1-\bar x=\frac{\mu_1-\mu_2}{2},\qquad \mu_2-\bar x=-\,\frac{\mu_1-\mu_2}{2}.$$

Feed those into a scatter measured from the global centre. Writing \(d=\mu_1-\mu_2\), and noting that the outer product squares away the sign on the second term:

$$\begin{aligned} N_1(\mu_1-\bar x)(\mu_1-\bar x)^{\top}+N_2(\mu_2-\bar x)(\mu_2-\bar x)^{\top} &=\frac{N}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{4}dd^{\top}+\frac{N}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{4}dd^{\top}\\[3pt] &=\frac{N}{8}dd^{\top}+\frac{N}{8}dd^{\top} \;=\;\frac{N}{4}\,dd^{\top}. \end{aligned}$$

The same rank-1 matrix as Phase 1, multiplied by a constant. And because Fisher's criterion is a ratio, a constant in the numerator cancels against nothing and changes nothing: the maximising direction is identical. The two formulations are not merely similar — they are the same objective.

The unbalanced case, which is the one you will meet

Nothing forces \(N_1=N_2\). Carrying the weights through with \(\bar x=(N_1\mu_1+N_2\mu_2)/N\) gives \(\mu_1-\bar x=\tfrac{N_2}{N}d\) and \(\mu_2-\bar x=-\tfrac{N_1}{N}d\), and the scatter comes out as

$$S_B=\frac{N_1N_2^2+N_2N_1^2}{N^2}\,dd^{\top}=\frac{N_1N_2}{N}\,dd^{\top}.$$

Still rank 1, still proportional to \(dd^{\top}\), only the constant changes. Setting \(N_1=N_2=N/2\) recovers \(N/4\), so the balanced result above is the special case. Verified numerically at splits of 50/50, 80/20 and 10000/5 — the identity holds exactly in every one.

PHASE 3 · THE GENERALISATION

Once "apart from each other" and "away from a shared centre" are the same thing, the general formula needs no defending:

$$S_B=\sum_{k=1}^{K} N_k\left(\mu_k-\bar x\right)\left(\mu_k-\bar x\right)^{\top}, \qquad \bar x=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K} N_k\mu_k .$$

The two new symbols are now forced rather than imposed:

  • The global mean \(\bar x\). With three or more classes there is no single "difference" to push along. You need a stake in the ground to push everything away from, and the centre of the data is the only choice that treats all classes alike.
  • The weight \(N_k\). If one class holds 10,000 points and another holds 5, moving the large one away from the centre shifts far more of the dataset's actual scatter. Weighting by \(N_k\) makes heavy classes exert proportionate pull, and it is also what makes \(S_B\) the genuine between-class half of the decomposition \(S_T=S_W+S_B\).
14

Step 3 — within-class scatter

Separating the means is not enough. If the clouds are wide in the same direction, they still overlap.

This is the step students most often skip, and the one that makes Fisher's criterion more than "point at the mean difference". Measure how tightly each class clusters around its own projected mean, and add the classes together:

$$S_W=\sum_{k}\ \sum_{i:\,y_i=k}\left(x_i-\mu_k\right)\left(x_i-\mu_k\right)^{\top} \qquad\text{(within-class scatter matrix)}$$

and the projected within-class spread is \(w^{\top}S_W\,w\). Note that this is the same matrix as the pooled covariance of block 10, up to the constant \(n-K\) — a point worth making explicitly, because it is the hinge on which block 16 turns.

The decomposition worth putting on the board

Total scatter splits cleanly into the two pieces:

$$S_T=\underbrace{\sum_i (x_i-\bar x)(x_i-\bar x)^{\top}}_{\text{everything}} = \underbrace{S_W}_{\text{spread within classes}}+\underbrace{S_B}_{\text{spread between classes}}$$

PCA maximises \(w^{\top}S_Tw\). Fisher maximises \(w^{\top}S_Bw / w^{\top}S_Ww\). Both are built from the same raw material; they differ in whether the labels are used to split it.

15

Step 4 — maximising the criterion

Combine the two goals into one ratio and differentiate.

$$J(w)=\frac{w^{\top}S_B\,w}{w^{\top}S_W\,w} \;=\;\frac{\text{separation between the projected classes}}{\text{spread within the projected classes}}$$

Because the scale of \(w\) cancels between numerator and denominator, \(J\) depends only on the direction of \(w\). In two dimensions it is therefore a function of a single angle, which is what makes it easy to plot.

Interactive · what \(w^{\top}S w\) is doing, one step at a time

A quadratic form is two operations, not one: first the matrix acts on \(w\) to give a vector, then that vector is dotted with \(w\) to give a number. Step through both for \(S_W\) and \(S_B\), then watch the ratio.

One \(\Sigma\), shared — so both ellipses change together. That is the LDA assumption. Set elongation to 1 and the optimum snaps to the mean-difference direction.

The maximisation

STEP 1 · DIFFERENTIATE THE RATIO

Write \(N=w^{\top}S_Bw\) and \(D=w^{\top}S_Ww\). Using \(\nabla_w(w^{\top}Aw)=2Aw\) for symmetric \(A\), the quotient rule gives

$$\nabla_w J=\frac{2S_Bw\,D-2S_Ww\,N}{D^{2}}\;\overset{!}{=}\;0 .$$
STEP 2 · RECOGNISE AN EIGENVALUE PROBLEM

Multiply through by \(D/2\) and rearrange:

$$S_Bw=\frac{N}{D}\,S_Ww=J(w)\,S_Ww .$$

This is a generalised eigenvalue problem \(S_Bw=\lambda S_Ww\), and the eigenvalue \(\lambda\) is the value of the criterion itself. Maximising \(J\) therefore means taking the eigenvector belonging to the largest eigenvalue.

STEP 3 · USE THE RANK-1 STRUCTURE OF \(S_B\)

For two classes we can solve it in closed form. Substitute \(S_B=(\mu_1-\mu_2)(\mu_1-\mu_2)^{\top}\) and note that \((\mu_1-\mu_2)^{\top}w\) is a scalar — call it \(c\):

$$S_Bw=(\mu_1-\mu_2)\underbrace{(\mu_1-\mu_2)^{\top}w}_{\textstyle c}=c\,(\mu_1-\mu_2).$$

So \(S_Bw\) always points along the mean difference, whatever \(w\) is.

STEP 4 · DROP THE SCALARS

We now have \(c\,(\mu_1-\mu_2)=\lambda\,S_Ww\). Since only the direction of \(w\) matters, both scalars can be discarded:

$$w^{\star}\ \propto\ S_W^{-1}(\mu_1-\mu_2).$$
What the answer says

Start with the mean difference — the naive direction — and then pre-multiply by \(S_W^{-1}\). That matrix whitens the space: it stretches directions in which the classes are narrow and compresses directions in which they are wide. The effect is to swing the projection away from directions that look promising but happen to be noisy. When \(S_W\propto I\) there is nothing to correct and \(w^{\star}\propto\mu_1-\mu_2\) after all.

The value achieved at the optimum is worth recording, because it is a familiar quantity in disguise:

$$J(w^{\star})=(\mu_1-\mu_2)^{\top}S_W^{-1}(\mu_1-\mu_2)=D^2_{\text{Mahalanobis}}.$$

Teaching order that works

Set the elongation slider to \(1\times\) first. The clouds are circular, the optimum sits exactly at the mean-difference angle, and students see the naive answer being correct. Now raise the elongation and rotate the orientation: the optimum walks away from the mean-difference angle, and the gap between the two \(J\) values opens up. The criterion is doing visible work.

16

Why Fisher and LDA agree

Two derivations, no shared assumptions, one direction.

Module 2 — probabilistic LDAModule 3 — Fisher
Starting pointGaussian class-conditionals, shared \(\Sigma\), Bayes' ruleA ratio of projected scatters. No distribution assumed.
Objectivemaximise the posteriormaximise \(J(w)\)
Direction obtained\(w=\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_1-\mu_2)\)\(w^{\star}\propto S_W^{-1}(\mu_1-\mu_2)\)

The two expressions are the same object. The pooled covariance estimate of block 10 is \(\hat\Sigma = S_W/(n-K)\), and a positive scalar does not change a direction, so

$$\hat\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_1-\mu_2)\ \propto\ S_W^{-1}(\mu_1-\mu_2).$$
What each derivation contributes that the other does not
  • Fisher gives the direction only. \(J\) is scale-invariant and has no notion of where along the line to cut. To classify you must add a threshold from somewhere else.
  • LDA gives the direction and the threshold. The constant \(b=-\tfrac12(\mu_1+\mu_2)^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_1-\mu_2)+\log(\pi_1/\pi_2)\) drops out of the probability model, priors included.
  • Fisher needs no Gaussian assumption. It is a statement about first and second moments, so it remains a sensible thing to optimise for non-Gaussian data — while LDA's optimality guarantee does not survive.

This is the honest summary for students: Fisher's criterion tells you where to look; the probability model tells you where to cut. LDA is the combination, and it is a small historical accident that one name covers both.

17

More than two classes

The rank of \(S_B\) puts a hard ceiling on how many discriminant directions exist.

With \(K\) classes, the between-class scatter is built from the deviations of the class means about the global mean, weighted by class size:

$$S_B=\sum_{k=1}^{K} n_k\left(\mu_k-\bar\mu\right)\left(\mu_k-\bar\mu\right)^{\top}, \qquad \bar\mu=\frac{1}{n}\sum_k n_k\mu_k .$$

The generalised eigenproblem \(S_Bw=\lambda S_Ww\) is unchanged, and its leading eigenvectors are the discriminant directions, taken in order of decreasing \(\lambda\).

At most \(K-1\) directions

The \(K\) vectors \(\mu_k-\bar\mu\) sum to zero after weighting, so they span a subspace of dimension at most \(K-1\). Hence \(\operatorname{rank}(S_B)\le K-1\), and \(S_W^{-1}S_B\) has at most \(K-1\) non-zero eigenvalues. Three classes in a 200-dimensional space can be projected to two dimensions with no loss of discriminative information — which is exactly why LDA is such an effective plotting tool for labelled data, and why the two-class case gives a single direction.

Practical failure mode

\(S_W\) must be inverted, and it is singular whenever \(n-Kregularised LDA), reduce dimension with PCA first, or use the pseudo-inverse. Any of these is better than the error message.

Consolidation
18

A worked example, by hand

Numbers chosen so every step comes out clean — and so the boundary lands somewhere students would not have guessed.

Two classes in \(\mathbb{R}^2\), equal priors:

$$\mu_1=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mu_2=\begin{pmatrix}5\\3\end{pmatrix},\qquad \Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\2&3\end{pmatrix},\qquad \pi_1=\pi_2=\tfrac12 .$$
Step 1 — invert the covariance

\(|\Sigma| = 4\cdot3-2\cdot2 = 8\), and for a \(2\times2\) matrix the inverse swaps the diagonal and negates the off-diagonal:

$$\Sigma^{-1}=\frac{1}{8}\begin{pmatrix}3&-2\\-2&4\end{pmatrix}.$$
Step 2 — the weight vector
$$\mu_1-\mu_2=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\-2\end{pmatrix},\qquad w=\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_1-\mu_2)=\frac{1}{8}\begin{pmatrix}3&-2\\-2&4\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}-4\\-2\end{pmatrix} =\frac{1}{8}\begin{pmatrix}-8\\0\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\0\end{pmatrix}.$$

Stop and look at this. The mean difference points down and to the left, at roughly \(27^\circ\) below horizontal. The weight vector points straight along the \(x_1\) axis. \(\Sigma^{-1}\) has rotated it by \(27^\circ\), and the second feature has dropped out of the decision entirely.

Step 3 — the intercept
$$b=-\tfrac12(\mu_1+\mu_2)^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_1-\mu_2)+\log\frac{\pi_1}{\pi_2} =-\tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}6\\4\end{pmatrix}^{\!\top}\begin{pmatrix}-1\\0\end{pmatrix}+\log 1 =-\tfrac12(-6)=3 .$$
Step 4 — the rule
$$w^{\top}x+b\ \ge 0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad -x_1+3\ \ge 0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x_1\le 3 .$$

The boundary is the vertical line \(x_1=3\). It passes through the midpoint \((3,2)\) of the two means, as it must with equal priors. But it is emphatically not the perpendicular bisector: the segment joining the means has slope \(\tfrac12\), so the bisector would have slope \(-2\), not infinity. Feature \(x_2\) is ignored, because once you account for its correlation with \(x_1\) it carries no additional discriminative information here.

Step 5 — cross-check with the discriminant functions
$$\delta_1(x)=0.125\,x_1+0.25\,x_2-0.1875+\log\pi_1,\qquad \delta_2(x)=1.125\,x_1+0.25\,x_2-3.1875+\log\pi_2 .$$

Subtracting: \(\delta_1-\delta_2=-x_1+3\). Same answer, and the \(x_2\) terms cancel because they are equal — a useful sanity check that also shows why \(x_2\) disappears.

Step 6 — Fisher's view of the same problem

Fisher's optimal direction is \(S_W^{-1}(\mu_1-\mu_2)\propto\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_1-\mu_2)=(-1,0)^{\top}\) — the same direction, reached without writing down a density. The value of the criterion there is

$$J(w^{\star})=(\mu_1-\mu_2)^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_1-\mu_2)=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\-2\end{pmatrix}^{\!\top}\begin{pmatrix}-1\\0\end{pmatrix}=4,$$

so the Mahalanobis distance between the classes is \(\sqrt{4}=2\). Fisher stops here. LDA continues and supplies the cut at \(x_1=3\).

Try it with unequal priors

Set \(\pi_1=0.7\). Then \(\log(\pi_1/\pi_2)=\log(7/3)\approx0.847\), so \(b\approx3.847\) and the boundary moves to \(x_1\approx3.85\). The line slides towards class 2, enlarging class 1's region — which is what a higher prior for class 1 should do. The direction is untouched: priors move the threshold, never the normal.

20

Exam-style practice

Attempt each before opening the answer. Several target the exact misconceptions flagged above.

Explain precisely which step of the LDA derivation fails if the classes have different covariance matrices.

Step 4. Expanding both quadratic forms produces \(-\tfrac12 x^{\top}\Sigma_k^{-1}x\) and \(+\tfrac12 x^{\top}\Sigma_\ell^{-1}x\). These cancel only when \(\Sigma_k=\Sigma_\ell\). Otherwise their difference \(\tfrac12 x^{\top}(\Sigma_\ell^{-1}-\Sigma_k^{-1})x\) survives, the log-odds becomes quadratic in \(x\), and the boundary is a conic. The normalising constants \(|\Sigma_k|^{-1/2}\) also stop cancelling, contributing \(-\tfrac12\log|\Sigma_k|\) to each discriminant.

\(\mu_1=(0,0)\), \(\mu_2=(2,2)\), \(\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&4\end{pmatrix}\), equal priors. Find \(w\) and \(b\). Is the boundary perpendicular to the segment joining the means?

\(\Sigma^{-1}=\operatorname{diag}(1,\tfrac14)\), so \(w=\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_1-\mu_2)=(-2,-\tfrac12)^{\top}\). Then \(b=-\tfrac12(\mu_1+\mu_2)^{\top}w=-\tfrac12\big[(2)(-2)+(2)(-\tfrac12)\big]=-\tfrac12(-5)=2.5\). Rule: \(-2x_1-0.5x_2+2.5\ge0\).

No. The mean difference points along \((1,1)\) at \(45^\circ\); the normal \(w\) points along \((4,1)\), about \(14^\circ\). Because \(x_2\) has four times the variance, movement along \(x_2\) is discounted fourfold, and the boundary tilts accordingly. It would be perpendicular only if \(\Sigma\propto I\).

A student computes \(\hat\Sigma\) by taking all \(n\) training points, subtracting the global mean, and averaging the outer products. What have they actually computed, and what will it do to the classifier?

They have computed the total scatter \(S_T=S_W+S_B\), not \(S_W\). The between-class term has been absorbed into what should measure within-class spread, so \(\hat\Sigma\) is inflated specifically in the direction \(\mu_1-\mu_2\).

Effect: \(\hat\Sigma^{-1}\) shrinks that direction, so the weight vector rotates towards the perpendicular bisector and the classifier discards some of the discriminative signal. Accuracy degrades most when the classes are well separated, because that is when \(S_B\) is large relative to \(S_W\).

Why is \(S_B\) rank 1 in the two-class case, and what does that imply about how many useful projection directions exist?

\(S_B=(\mu_1-\mu_2)(\mu_1-\mu_2)^{\top}\) is an outer product of a single vector with itself, so its column space is the one-dimensional span of \(\mu_1-\mu_2\), giving rank 1 and exactly one non-zero eigenvalue. Consequently \(S_W^{-1}S_B\) has one non-zero eigenvalue and there is exactly one discriminant direction. Any direction orthogonal to \(\mu_1-\mu_2\) gives \(w^{\top}S_Bw=0\) and hence \(J=0\) — the projected means coincide. In general \(\operatorname{rank}(S_B)\le K-1\), so \(K\) classes give at most \(K-1\) directions.

Derive \(w^{\star}\propto S_W^{-1}(\mu_1-\mu_2)\) from \(J(w)=\dfrac{w^{\top}S_Bw}{w^{\top}S_Ww}\).

Setting \(\nabla_wJ=0\) with \(N=w^{\top}S_Bw\), \(D=w^{\top}S_Ww\) gives \(2S_BwD-2S_WwN=0\), i.e. \(S_Bw=(N/D)S_Ww=\lambda S_Ww\) — a generalised eigenproblem whose eigenvalue is the criterion value.

For two classes, \(S_Bw=(\mu_1-\mu_2)\big[(\mu_1-\mu_2)^{\top}w\big]\), and the bracket is a scalar, so \(S_Bw\) always points along \(\mu_1-\mu_2\). Thus \(\lambda S_Ww\propto\mu_1-\mu_2\), and multiplying by \(S_W^{-1}\) and dropping scalars gives \(w^{\star}\propto S_W^{-1}(\mu_1-\mu_2)\).

Fisher's criterion is scale-invariant. Why does that matter, and what does it prevent Fisher from telling you?

Replacing \(w\) by \(cw\) multiplies numerator and denominator by \(c^2\), leaving \(J\) unchanged. This is convenient — the optimisation is over directions, not vectors, so no normalisation constraint is strictly needed — but it means the solution carries no information about where along the projected axis to place the threshold. Fisher gives a direction only. The cut point must come from elsewhere: the Gaussian model with priors (LDA), or empirically by minimising training error on the projected values.

When do PCA and Fisher's LDA return the same direction, and why is relying on that dangerous?

When the within-class scatter is isotropic, \(S_W\propto I\). Then \(S_W^{-1}(\mu_1-\mu_2)\propto\mu_1-\mu_2\), and if the classes are also well separated the dominant structure in \(S_T=S_W+S_B\) is \(S_B\), so the top principal component aligns with the mean difference too.

Dangerous because PCA has no mechanism to notice when this fails. If the within-class spread is large along some direction unrelated to the class difference — which is the common case with correlated features — PCA will happily return that direction and the projected classes will overlap completely. See the figure in block 11, where the two answers are nearly perpendicular.

You have 40 training points, 2 classes, 30 features. Would you fit LDA or QDA? Justify with parameter counts.

LDA, and even that needs care. QDA must estimate \(K\,p(p+1)/2 = 2\times465=930\) covariance parameters from 40 points, with each class's \(\hat\Sigma_k\) built from only 20 points in 30 dimensions — guaranteed singular, so QDA cannot even be fitted. LDA pools to \(465\) parameters estimated from all 40 points, which is still \(n-K=38 < p=30\)... in fact also singular.

The honest answer: neither works unmodified. You need regularisation (\(\hat\Sigma+\gamma I\)), dimension reduction first, or a diagonal-covariance restriction — which is Gaussian naive Bayes, needing only \(p=30\) variance parameters. This is precisely the regime where the "naive" assumption earns its place.

The prior for class 1 changes from 0.5 to 0.9. What happens to \(w\), to \(b\), and to the boundary?

\(w=\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_1-\mu_2)\) contains no prior, so it is unchanged — the boundary does not rotate. \(b\) gains \(\log(0.9/0.1)=\log 9\approx2.197\) relative to the equal-prior case, so the hyperplane translates parallel to itself, moving away from \(\mu_1\) and enlarging class 1's region. In the block 18 example the boundary would move from \(x_1=3\) to \(x_1\approx5.2\), putting even \(\mu_2=(5,3)\) on class 1's side — correct behaviour when class 2 is only one point in ten.

Show that with equal priors, LDA is equivalent to "assign \(x\) to the class whose mean is nearest in Mahalanobis distance".

Start from \(\log f_k(x)\pi_k\) and drop terms that are identical across classes — \(-\tfrac{p}{2}\log2\pi\) and \(-\tfrac12\log|\Sigma|\), both class-free under shared \(\Sigma\):

\(\delta_k(x)=-\tfrac12(x-\mu_k)^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu_k)+\log\pi_k\).

With \(\pi_k\) equal, \(\log\pi_k\) is a common constant too, so maximising \(\delta_k\) is minimising \((x-\mu_k)^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu_k)\), the squared Mahalanobis distance to \(\mu_k\). Expanding this form and dropping the shared \(x^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}x\) recovers the linear version in block 8 — the two are the same rule written differently. With unequal priors it becomes nearest-mean plus an additive bonus of \(\log\pi_k\).

Scope. This document follows a three-module sequence: the probabilistic foundation, the Gaussian assumption and its linear consequence, and Fisher's projection view. Every derivation is carried out in full rather than asserted, and the two interactive panels recompute their contents from the sliders, so the numbers shown are always the ones the current configuration implies.

Further reading. Fisher, The Use of Multiple Measurements in Taxonomic Problems (1936) — the original, and still readable. Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning, §4.3 for LDA, reduced-rank LDA and the QDA comparison. Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, §4.1 for Fisher's criterion and its least-squares connection. Friedman, Regularized Discriminant Analysis (1989) for the \(\alpha\)-dial between LDA and QDA.
